Definition: Affordability of electricity for residential and small business consumers, measured as cost of electricity relative to income levels. High electricity costs are a direct barrier to ICT adoption and data center viability.
Comments: No data found after thorough searching
redteam_note: Scored 0/Unknown with no source — confirm it is truly unknown, not just unresearched. No data year recorded — provenance/recency unknown.
revision_notes: A light check surfaced an authoritative World Bank source with actual tariff data, so this row was moved to the full verification path. The World Bank's Guinea-Bissau Power Sector Policy Note gives an average utility (EAGB) tariff of around US$0.38/kWh (2019-20), corroborated by an independent solar-market report. Applying EAGB's lowest 'social' block tariff (81 FCFA/kWh, capped at 50 kWh/month, plus a 1,500 FCFA/month fixed charge) gives a minimum residential bill of roughly US$9/month. Against a 2024 GNI per capita of US$990 (about US$82.50/month, World Bank Atlas method), this is approximately 11% of monthly per-capita income, i.e. Value Code 1 (Very Expensive, >10% of GNI p.c.). This is consistent with independent commentary (cited via a Bissau resident's blog referencing L'Economiste du Faso) describing Guinea-Bissau as among the three most expensive electricity markets in the ECOWAS region. Because this figure rests on a calculated estimate combining a 2019-20 tariff schedule with 2024 income data rather than a single published affordability index, it is flagged for human review to confirm the exact banding.
revised_comments: Electricity is among the most expensive in the ECOWAS region: the state utility EAGB charges an average tariff of around US$0.38/kWh, and even the cheapest residential 'social' tariff block equates to roughly US$9 per month for a minimal consumption allowance. Against a GNI per capita of around US$990 in 2024 (about US$82.50/month), this represents more than 10% of average monthly income for even a basic electricity package, placing affordability in the 'very expensive' band.
